newsitem.title: USA: Good weather drives down energy, grain prices.
newsitem.headline: Good weather drives down energy, grain prices.

text.p: Oil and natural gas prices dropped sharply and grain prices fell Monday as better-than-expected weather helped crops and eased the demand for heating fuels.
The Knight Ridder Commodity Research index of 17 commodity futures ended down 1.89 points to 243.81.
Oil prices at the New York Mercantile Exchange dropped after the Midwest and Northeast enjoyed warmer-than-predicted weather over the weekend.
As the unusually mild weather continued Monday, January heating oil led the drop in energy prices, ending 1.89 cents a gallon lower at 71.08 cents.
January gasoline fell 1.29 cents a gallon to 68.90 cents, and February crude oil closed 29 cents a barrel at $24.79.
Natural gas, which had soared recently, dropped 38.1 cents to $4.192 per million British thermal units for the January contract.

Forecaster Weather Services Corp. and others predicted temperatures through Tuesday to average 6 to 15 degrees above normal and to average near normal through Friday in the key Northeast heating oil market.

With Iraqi crude oil sales flowing again as of last week and Russian fuel exports also rising, supply worries are fading. About 180,000 metric tons (1.3 million barrels) of Russian heating oil is due in the United States this week.

"There is supply floating about the Atlantic looking for a home while temperatures seem to be moderating. That's a combination for some pretty good profit-taking," said James Cordier, a trader with Allendale Inc.
Weather also played the key role in grain markets.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, January soybeans fell 2 cents a bushel to close at $7.00, with heavy speculative selling in soybean oil adding to the decline.
January soy oil closed down 0.30 cent a pound at 22.79 cents.

"Good weather in the U.S. and South America was the main thing," said analyst Vic Lespinasse of Dean Witter Reynolds. "But it was a very dull day and tomorrow probably will be more of the same, just shorter."
Most futures markets close early on Christmas Eve.
Wheat prices fell due to ideal snow cover in the High Plains and lower-than-expected export demand. March wheat fell 2-3/4 cents a bushel to $3.90-1/2.

A weekly Agriculture Department report on export demand showed only 13.3 million bushels of wheat inspected for export for the week ended Dec. 19, near the low end of forecasts of 12 million to 16 million bushels.
March corn fell 1/4 cent to $2.66-1/2, pressured by weakness in other grains but boosted by the recent cold weather in the central United States that boosted demand for animal feed.

At the New York Cotton Exchange, frozen concentrated orange juice futures settled sharply lower and barely above new contract lows as cold weather appeared likely to avoid the Florida citrus belt for now, dealers said.
March frozen concentrated orange juice futures ended down 4.5 cents at 86.20 cents a pound.
